questions.subject: regs
questions.question: A steady green light from the tower to an aircraft in flight means…
options: Give way to other aircraft and keep circling
questions.explanation: In flight: steady green = cleared to land; flashing green = return for landing; steady red = give way and keep circling; flashing red = aerodrome unsafe, do not land.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: A flashing red light from the tower to an aircraft on the ground means…
options: Return to starting point on the aerodrome
Taxi clear of the landing area in use
questions.explanation: On the ground: steady red = stop; flashing red = taxi clear of the landing area in use; flashing white = return to starting point; steady green = cleared for take-off; flashing green = cleared to taxi.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Two aircraft are converging at about the same level. Which one gives way?
options: The one that has the other on its left
The one that has the other on its right
questions.explanation: When converging at about the same level, the aircraft that has the other on its right gives way (subject to the order of right of way between aircraft types).

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Two aircraft are approaching head-on. What should each do?
options: The one with the faster speed climbs
Both alter heading to the right
questions.explanation: Head-on or nearly head-on with danger of collision: each alters its heading to the right.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: An aircraft overtaking another keeps out of the way by…
questions.explanation: The aircraft being overtaken has the right of way. The overtaking aircraft keeps out of the way by altering its heading to the right, whether climbing, descending or level.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: A power-driven heavier-than-air aircraft must give way to…
options: No one — it always has right of way
questions.explanation: Order of giving way: power-driven heavier-than-air gives way to airships, gliders and balloons; airships give way to gliders and balloons; gliders give way to balloons. Aircraft towing objects are also given way to.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: In India, VFR flights normally operate…
options: From 20 minutes before sunrise to 20 minutes after sunset
From 30 minutes before sunrise to 30 minutes after sunset
At any time with an ATC clearance
questions.explanation: VFR flights in India operate from 20 minutes before sunrise to 20 minutes after sunset, except local flights and flying club training flights exempted by ATC.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Unless authorised by ATS, VFR flights shall not be operated above…
questions.explanation: VFR is not allowed above FL150, at transonic or supersonic speeds, or more than 100 NM seaward in controlled airspace, unless authorised by the ATS authority.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Minimum height for a VFR flight over a congested area of a city is…
options: 1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 600 m
1500 ft above the highest obstacle within 1 km
2000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km
questions.explanation: Over congested areas or open-air assemblies: 300 m (1000 ft) above the highest obstacle within a radius of 600 m. Elsewhere: 150 m (500 ft) above ground or water.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Away from congested areas, a VFR flight must not be flown lower than…
questions.explanation: Elsewhere (not congested), VFR flight must stay at least 150 m (500 ft) above the ground or water, except for take-off and landing.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Without an ATC clearance, VFR flight may not take off or land at an aerodrome in a control zone when…
options: Ceiling is below 2000 ft or ground visibility below 8 km
Ceiling is below 1500 ft or ground visibility below 5 km
Ceiling is below 1000 ft or ground visibility below 3 km
Ceiling is below 3000 ft or ground visibility below 5 km
questions.explanation: The limits are a ceiling of 450 m (1500 ft) and ground visibility of 5 km. Below either, a VFR flight needs an ATC clearance to take off, land or enter the traffic pattern there.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: The nationality mark for civil aircraft registered in India is…
questions.explanation: Indian civil aircraft carry 'VT' followed by a hyphen and three letters (e.g. VT-EPC). 'VU' is used for Air Force aircraft. India was allotted AT–AW by the ITU but kept VT.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: On the wings of a heavier-than-air aircraft, registration marks must be at least…
questions.explanation: Marks on the wings must be at least 50 cm high; on the fuselage and vertical tail surfaces at least 30 cm.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Minimum age to hold a CPL in India is…
questions.explanation: Minimum ages: SPL 16, PPL 17, CPL 18, ATPL 21.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Since October 2023, Indian pilot licences are valid for…
questions.explanation: All licences are valid for 10 years from the date of issue since 10 Oct 2023. Renewal is done from the expiry date if applied for within one month before expiry.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Who may have sole control of an aircraft in motion?
options: Only a person who has reached 18 years
Anyone holding a student pilot licence, at any age
Only a person who has reached 16 years
questions.explanation: No person under 16 shall have sole control of an aircraft in motion.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: An aircraft squawking 7600 is reporting…
questions.explanation: 7500 = unlawful interference, 7600 = radio communication failure, 7700 = emergency.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Squawk 7500 means…
questions.explanation: 7500 = unlawful interference. Remember: 75 'taken alive', 76 'radio fix', 77 'going to heaven'.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: The Chicago Convention was signed on…
questions.explanation: Signed at Chicago on 7 December 1944; it came into force on 4 April 1947, which is when ICAO was formally established. ICAO's headquarters are in Montreal.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: ICAO Annex 2 covers…
questions.explanation: Annex 1 Personnel Licensing, Annex 2 Rules of the Air, Annex 3 Meteorology, Annex 14 Aerodromes.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Aircraft accident and incident investigation is covered by…
questions.explanation: Annex 11 Air Traffic Services, Annex 12 Search and Rescue, Annex 13 Aircraft Accident and Incident Investigation, Annex 17 Security.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Search and Rescue is covered by…
questions.explanation: Annex 10 Aeronautical Telecommunications, Annex 12 Search and Rescue, Annex 15 Aeronautical Information Services, Annex 18 Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Security against acts of unlawful interference is covered by…
questions.explanation: Annex 9 Facilitation, Annex 16 Environmental Protection, Annex 17 Security, Annex 19 Safety Management.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: The fifth freedom of the air is the right to…
options: Carry traffic between two foreign States on a service to or from your own State
Land in another State for non-traffic purposes
Carry traffic between two points inside a foreign State
Fly across another State without landing
questions.explanation: 1st: overfly. 2nd: technical stop. 3rd: set down traffic from home State. 4th: pick up traffic bound for home State. 5th: carry traffic between two foreign States on a service that starts or ends at home. Cabotage is carrying traffic within another State.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: An aircraft is in the HEAVY wake turbulence category when its MTOW is…
questions.explanation: Heavy: 136,000 kg or more. Medium: more than 7,000 kg and less than 136,000 kg. Light: 7,000 kg or less. (The A380 is classed 'Super'.)

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: A LIGHT aircraft has an MTOW of…
questions.explanation: Light: 7,000 kg or less. Don't mix this up with 5,700 kg, which is used for other purposes (e.g. aeroplane categories in airworthiness).

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Radar wake turbulence separation on approach: LIGHT behind HEAVY is…
questions.explanation: Radar wake minima: Heavy behind Heavy 4 NM, Medium behind Heavy 5 NM, Light behind Heavy 6 NM, Light behind Medium 5 NM.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: DETRESFA is the…
questions.explanation: INCERFA = uncertainty, ALERFA = alert, DETRESFA = distress.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: On a ground-to-air signal panel, the symbol V means…
questions.explanation: V = require assistance; X = require medical assistance; arrow = proceeding in this direction; Y = yes; N = no.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: For accident reporting, a fatal injury is one resulting in death within…
questions.explanation: A fatal injury is one that results in death within 30 days of the accident.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: A serious injury includes hospitalisation for more than…
options: 48 hours, starting within 30 days of the injury
72 hours, starting within 10 days of the injury
48 hours, starting within 7 days of the injury
24 hours, starting within 3 days of the injury
questions.explanation: Serious injury includes hospitalisation for more than 48 hours, commencing within 7 days from the date the injury was received (plus fractures, severe burns etc.).

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: 'PAN PAN' indicates…
options: Distress: grave and imminent danger, immediate help needed
Urgency: a condition concerning safety, no immediate help needed
questions.explanation: MAYDAY = distress (grave and imminent danger, immediate assistance required). PAN PAN = urgency (concerning safety of an aircraft or person, no immediate assistance required).

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: The aeronautical VHF emergency frequency is…
questions.explanation: 121.5 MHz is the VHF emergency frequency. 243.0 MHz is the military UHF emergency frequency.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: On the readability scale, '5' means…
questions.explanation: 1 unreadable, 2 readable now and then, 3 readable but with difficulty, 4 readable, 5 perfectly readable.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: By day, an intercepted aircraft acknowledges 'You have been intercepted, follow me' by…
questions.explanation: Intercepting aircraft rocks its wings and makes a slow level turn; the intercepted aircraft rocks its wings and follows. At night it also flashes its navigation lights.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Runway designation numbers are based on…
options: Magnetic direction to the nearest 10°, divided by 10
questions.explanation: The runway number is its magnetic direction rounded to the nearest 10°, then divided by 10 (e.g. 274° M → 27).

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: On approach, PAPI shows two white and two red lights. You are…
questions.explanation: 4 white = too high; 3 white 1 red = slightly high; 2 white 2 red = on slope; 1 white 3 red = slightly low; 4 red = too low.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Taxiway edge lights are…
questions.explanation: Taxiway edge lights are blue; taxiway centreline lights are green.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Runway threshold lights are…
questions.explanation: Threshold lights are green (seen from the approach); runway end lights are red.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: A standard holding pattern uses…
options: Right turns, 1½-minute inbound leg at or below 14,000 ft
Right turns, 1-minute inbound leg at or below 14,000 ft
questions.explanation: Standard holds are right-hand. Inbound leg is 1 minute at or below 14,000 ft and 1½ minutes above 14,000 ft.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Above the transition level, the altimeter is set to…
questions.explanation: Climbing through the transition altitude, set 1013.2 hPa and fly flight levels. Descending through the transition level, set QNH and fly altitudes.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: With QFE set, the altimeter on the aerodrome reads…
questions.explanation: QFE: reads height above the aerodrome (zero on the ground). QNH: reads altitude above MSL (aerodrome elevation on the ground).

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: An IFR flight on a magnetic track of 090° flies at…
questions.explanation: Tracks 000°–179°: odd thousands (e.g. FL70, FL90). Tracks 180°–359°: even thousands. VFR adds 500 ft.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Minimum IFR level over normal terrain is…
options: 2000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km
500 ft above the highest obstacle within 5 km
1000 ft above the highest obstacle within 8 km
questions.explanation: IFR: at least 300 m (1000 ft) above the highest obstacle within 8 km of the estimated position; 600 m (2000 ft) over high terrain or in mountainous areas.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: A controlled flight's plan must be amended or re-filed when it is delayed by more than…
questions.explanation: Delay of 30 minutes beyond EOBT for a controlled flight (60 minutes for an uncontrolled flight) means the flight plan must be amended or a new one filed and the old one cancelled.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: In the SHELL model, the 'L' at the centre stands for…
questions.explanation: Software, Hardware, Environment, Liveware. The central Liveware is the pilot; the edges show how the person interacts with each element (including other Liveware).

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: The 'Swiss cheese' model of accident causation was developed by…
questions.explanation: James Reason's model shows accidents when holes in several layers of defences line up. Edwards created the SHEL model; Hawkins added the second L.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: 'Empty-field myopia' is when…
options: Night vision is lost after a bright light
The eyes relax to a short focus when there's nothing to look at
Glare off cloud tops dazzles the pilot
The runway looks narrower than it is
questions.explanation: With nothing to focus on (haze, cloud tops, featureless sky), the eyes settle at about 1–2 m, so distant traffic is missed. Fix: focus on a distant object like a wingtip, then scan.

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: Hypoxia from the low partial pressure of oxygen at altitude is called…
questions.explanation: Hypoxic: low partial pressure of O2 (altitude). Hypemic (anaemic): blood can't carry O2 (e.g. CO poisoning). Stagnant: poor circulation (e.g. g-forces). Histotoxic: cells can't use O2 (alcohol, drugs).

questions.subject: regs
questions.question: A strong forward acceleration on take-off can give the false sensation of…
questions.explanation: The somatogravic illusion: acceleration feels like a nose-up pitch, so a pilot in poor visibility may wrongly push the nose down.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: One nautical mile is…
options: 1 minute of arc of a great circle
questions.explanation: 1 NM is the length of 1 minute of arc along a great circle (1° = 60 NM). A minute of longitude only equals 1 NM on the equator.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: One nautical mile is about…
questions.explanation: 1 NM = 1,852 m (6,080 ft). 1 statute mile = 1,609 m.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: The shortest distance between two points on the Earth is along…
questions.explanation: A great circle (a circle whose centre is the Earth's centre) gives the shortest route. A rhumb line is easier to fly (constant direction) but longer.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: A rhumb line…
options: Crosses all meridians at the same angle
questions.explanation: A rhumb line cuts every meridian at the same angle, so its direction stays constant. Meridians and the equator are both rhumb lines and great circles.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Magnetic variation is the angle between…
questions.explanation: Variation: true vs magnetic north (changes with place). Deviation: magnetic vs compass north (caused by the aircraft's own magnetism).

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: True track 100°, variation 5°W. The magnetic track is…
questions.explanation: 'Variation west, magnetic best; variation east, magnetic least.' 100 + 5 = 105°M.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: A line joining places of zero variation is called…
questions.explanation: Agonic = zero variation. Isogonal = equal variation. Aclinic = zero dip (magnetic equator). Isoclinal = equal dip.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Magnetic dip is zero at…
questions.explanation: Dip is zero at the magnetic equator and 90° at the magnetic poles, where the horizontal field (and the compass) is useless.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: After 60 NM you are 4 NM off track. Your track error is about…
questions.explanation: 1 in 60 rule: 1 NM off in 60 NM ≈ 1°. Track error = distance off × 60 ÷ distance gone = 4 × 60 ÷ 60 = 4°.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: 2 NM off track after 30 NM, with 60 NM to go. Alter heading by how much to reach destination?
questions.explanation: Track error = 2 × 60 ÷ 30 = 4°. Closing angle = 2 × 60 ÷ 60 = 2°. Total alteration = 4 + 2 = 6°.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: At 60°N, 60 minutes of change of longitude equals a departure of…
questions.explanation: Departure = change of longitude (minutes) × cos latitude = 60 × cos 60° = 60 × 0.5 = 30 NM.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Flying at a constant CAS, as you climb your TAS…
questions.explanation: Air density falls with height, so for the same CAS the TAS is higher. Rule of thumb: TAS ≈ CAS + 2% per 1,000 ft.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Using the 2%-per-1,000 ft rule, CAS 100 kt at 10,000 ft is roughly…
questions.explanation: 10,000 ft × 2% per 1,000 ft = +20%, so about 120 kt TAS. Use the computer for the exact answer.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: With the wind blowing from your left, you will drift…
questions.explanation: The wind pushes you downwind, i.e. to the right. To hold track, head into the wind (a little to the left).

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: The three vectors of the triangle of velocities are heading/TAS, wind velocity and…
questions.explanation: Air vector (heading/TAS) + wind vector (W/V) = ground vector (track/GS).

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: You cover 150 NM in 50 minutes. Your groundspeed is…

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Near sea level, 1 hPa of pressure difference is taken as about…
questions.explanation: In the exam, 1 hPa ≈ 27 ft (some texts use 30 ft). E.g. QNH 1003: pressure altitude = elevation + (1013 − 1003) × 27.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: 15° of longitude is equal to…
questions.explanation: The Earth turns 360° in 24 hours: 15° = 1 hour, 1° = 4 minutes, 1' = 4 seconds.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Indian Standard Time is…
questions.explanation: IST = UTC + 5 h 30 min (based on 82°30'E). Aviation uses UTC, so subtract 5:30 from IST.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: On a 1:500,000 chart, 1 cm represents…

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: On a Mercator chart, which is a straight line?
questions.explanation: Mercator: meridians parallel, rhumb lines are straight, great circles curve toward the pole. Scale increases with sec latitude.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Scale on a Mercator chart varies as…
questions.explanation: Mercator scale = scale at the equator × sec latitude, so it expands away from the equator.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: On a Lambert's conformal chart, great circles are…
questions.explanation: Lambert's: a great circle is very nearly a straight line (slightly concave toward the parallel of origin), and the chart is conformal.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Earth convergency between two meridians equals change of longitude ×…
questions.explanation: Earth convergency = ch long × sin mean latitude. Conversion angle = ½ convergency.

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Northern hemisphere, heading east, accelerating: the compass shows an apparent turn towards…
questions.explanation: ANDS: Accelerate → North, Decelerate → South (northern hemisphere, on easterly or westerly headings).

questions.subject: gnav
questions.question: Northern hemisphere, turning off a northerly heading, the compass at first…
options: Lags, or even shows a turn the wrong way
Sticks on north for the whole turn
questions.explanation: Through north the compass is sluggish (undershoot the roll-out); through south it is lively and leads (overshoot the roll-out), in the northern hemisphere.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: Radio waves travel at about…
questions.explanation: c ≈ 3 × 10⁸ m/s = 300,000 km/s (about 162,000 NM/s). Wavelength = c ÷ frequency.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: The wavelength of a 300 MHz signal is…

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: VHF signals mainly travel by…
questions.explanation: VHF and above: line of sight. LF/MF: surface waves. HF: sky waves.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: Maximum VHF range for an aircraft at 10,000 ft from a station at sea level is about…
questions.explanation: Range (NM) ≈ 1.23 × (√transmitter height + √receiver height in ft) = 1.23 × √10,000 = 123 NM.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: NDBs operate in the…
questions.explanation: NDBs use LF/MF. VOR is VHF; DME is UHF.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: The ADF needle shows…
questions.explanation: ADF gives relative bearing (from the nose). Magnetic bearing to the station (QDM) = magnetic heading + relative bearing.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: Magnetic heading 040°, ADF relative bearing 090°. The QDM is…

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: ADF bearings are least reliable around dusk and dawn because of…
questions.explanation: Night effect: sky waves return and interfere with the surface wave, worst around dusk and dawn.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: VORs operate in the band…
questions.explanation: VOR is VHF, 108–117.975 MHz (the 108–112 MHz part is shared with ILS localisers).

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: A VOR radial is…
options: The magnetic bearing FROM the station
The true bearing TO the station
The magnetic bearing TO the station
questions.explanation: Radial = QDR, magnetic bearing from the VOR. Bearing to the station = QDM.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: The VOR receiver finds bearing by comparing…
options: The phase of a reference and a variable signal
questions.explanation: The phase difference between the reference (30 Hz FM) and variable (30 Hz AM) signals equals the radial.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: On a VOR deviation indicator, full-scale deflection represents…
questions.explanation: VOR full scale is always 10°: each dot is 2° on a 5-dot display, 5° on a 2-dot display. Compare ILS: localiser about 2.5°, glide path about 0.7°.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: ILS localiser full-scale deflection means you are at least…
options: 2.5° left or right of the centreline
questions.explanation: Localiser full scale ≈ 2.5° either side; glide path full scale ≈ 0.7° above or below.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: The ILS glide path transmits in the…
questions.explanation: Localiser: VHF 108–111.975 MHz (odd tenths). Glide path: UHF 329–335 MHz, paired with the localiser.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: The outer marker is shown by…
options: A blue light, 2 dashes a second, 400 Hz
An amber light, alternate dots and dashes, 1300 Hz
questions.explanation: OM: blue, 2 dashes/s, 400 Hz. MM: amber, dot-dash, 1300 Hz. IM: white, dots, 3000 Hz. All on 75 MHz.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: Primary radar detects a target by…
options: Receiving its own pulses reflected back
questions.explanation: Primary radar relies on echoes, so it needs nothing on board. SSR needs a transponder to reply.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: SSR interrogates on… and the aircraft replies on…
questions.explanation: Ground interrogates on 1030 MHz; transponder replies on 1090 MHz.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: SSR Mode C provides…
questions.explanation: Mode A = identity (4-digit code). Mode C = pressure altitude (referenced to 1013.25 hPa). Mode S adds selective addressing and data.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: DME operates in the…
questions.explanation: DME: UHF 962–1213 MHz, 1 MHz spacing, 252 channels; paired with VOR/ILS frequencies.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: DME measures…
questions.explanation: DME gives slant range. The error is largest when high and close to the station (overhead at 6,000 ft, DME reads about 1 NM).

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: Airborne weather radar shows best…
options: Large water droplets and wet hail
questions.explanation: It detects precipitation, strongest from large wet droplets and wet hail. It can't see CAT or dry particles well.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: Airborne weather radar uses a frequency of about…
questions.explanation: Around 9.4 GHz (X band, about 3 cm wavelength) — a good size for reflecting off raindrops.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: The minimum number of satellites for a 3D GPS fix is…
questions.explanation: 4 satellites for latitude, longitude, altitude and the receiver clock error. RAIM needs 5 to detect a fault, 6 to exclude it.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: RAIM is…
options: The receiver checking integrity using extra satellites
questions.explanation: Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring: the receiver uses redundant satellites to spot a faulty one.

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: GPS satellites orbit at about…
questions.explanation: GPS: about 20,200 km, roughly 12-hour orbits. 36,000 km is geostationary (used by SBAS satellites).

questions.subject: rnav
questions.question: A VDF bearing is obtained when…
options: The pilot transmits and the ground station measures the direction
The aircraft measures a ground beacon
questions.explanation: VHF Direction Finding: the ground station takes a bearing on the aircraft's transmission and passes QDM/QDR etc.

interview.question: On approach, you think the captain has set the wrong altitude. What do you do?
interview.covers: Speak up early and clearly, using the captain's name and the fact ("Captain, cleared 3000, 4000 is set")|Follow the escalation ladder: query, suggest, then state firmly or take action if safety is at risk|Keep it about the error, not the person|Why it matters: most accidents involve a missed chance to speak up (CRM, assertiveness)

interview.question: The weather at destination drops below minimums while you're holding. Fuel is getting low. Walk us through your thinking.
interview.covers: Know your fuel: minimum diversion fuel and final reserve|Decide before fuel decides for you: set a 'bingo' time to divert|Use a decision model like FORDEC (Facts, Options, Risks, Decision, Execution, Check)|Declare MINIMUM FUEL or MAYDAY FUEL as the rules require|Brief the cabin and passengers

interview.question: A passenger becomes unruly and refuses to sit down during taxi. What do you do?
interview.covers: The cockpit door stays closed — the flight crew don't leave the flight deck|Cabin crew handle it, with the captain's authority behind them|Options: stop and return to stand, involve security|Follow company procedures and report it

interview.question: You've finished your duty and are tired, but crew scheduling asks you to fly one more sector. What do you say?
interview.covers: Fatigue is a safety issue, not a weakness|Know the flight duty time limits (DGCA CAR on FDTL)|Say no politely if you're not fit, and report fatigue through the proper channel|Show you'd still help find a solution

interview.question: During take-off roll at 80 knots you get an amber caution. What happens?
interview.covers: Know your airline's 'low speed' vs 'high speed' regimes and V1|Below 100 kt you'd usually reject for any failure; above it only for serious ones|Callouts and who decides (the captain calls 'STOP' or 'GO')|After V1 you continue and deal with it in the air

interview.question: You notice your captain smells of alcohol before a flight. What do you do?
interview.covers: Safety first: the flight should not go with an impaired pilot|Raise it privately and respectfully first if possible|If not resolved, report to the company (duty manager / chief pilot)|Mention DGCA's pre-flight breath analyser checks

interview.question: Tell us about a time you made a mistake in training. What did you learn?
interview.covers: Pick a real, small mistake — not a disaster and not a fake one|STAR: Situation, Task, Action, Result|Focus on what you changed afterwards|Shows honesty and a learning mindset (just culture)

interview.question: Halfway to destination a passenger has a medical emergency. What are your options?
interview.covers: Ask cabin crew for details and for a doctor on board|Consider diverting to the nearest suitable airport|Declare PAN PAN or MAYDAY as appropriate and coordinate with ATC|Weigh weather, fuel and medical facilities at the options

interview.question: You disagree with the captain's decision but it's not unsafe. What do you do?
interview.covers: Voice your view once, clearly, with reasons|Accept the captain's authority if it's within safe limits|Debrief it afterwards|Shows teamwork and respect for the chain of command

interview.question: ATC gives you a clearance you're not sure you heard correctly. What do you do?
interview.covers: Never guess — ask 'Say again' or read back what you think and ask for confirmation|Check with the other pilot|Why: readback errors are a known cause of altitude busts

interview.question: Describe a stressful situation and how you handled it.
interview.covers: STAR format|What you felt and what you did to stay calm (breathing, checklists, prioritising)|Aviate, navigate, communicate|What the result was and what you'd do again

interview.question: You're flying with a captain who is very quiet and doesn't brief properly. How do you work with them?
interview.covers: Take the initiative: ask questions and brief your own parts|Keep the flight deck gradient comfortable — not too steep, not too flat|Use standard calls to build a shared picture|Stay professional, no complaining

interview.question: What is V1?
interview.covers: Take-off decision speed: the highest speed at which you can still reject the take-off and stop on the runway|After V1 you must continue|Compare VR (rotation) and V2 (take-off safety speed)

interview.question: Explain the difference between IAS, CAS, TAS and groundspeed.
interview.covers: IAS: read off the instrument|CAS: IAS corrected for instrument and position errors|TAS: CAS corrected for density (and compressibility) — speed through the air|GS: TAS corrected for wind — speed over the ground

interview.question: What are the four forces in flight and what happens in a steady climb?
interview.covers: Lift, weight, thrust, drag|In a steady climb, lift is slightly less than weight; part of the weight is balanced by thrust|Climb performance depends on excess thrust (angle) and excess power (rate)

interview.question: What causes a stall, and how do you recover?
interview.covers: Exceeding the critical angle of attack — it can happen at any speed or attitude|Recovery: reduce angle of attack (nose down) first, then roll wings level, then power|Know stall warning signs and the effect of weight, load factor and flaps on stall speed

interview.question: What is the difference between QNH, QFE and standard pressure, and when is each used?
interview.covers: QNH: altitude above MSL, used below transition altitude|QFE: height above the aerodrome|1013.2 hPa: flight levels above transition|Where the transition altitude and level are

interview.question: Explain how an ILS works.
interview.covers: Localiser: lateral guidance, VHF 108–112 MHz|Glide path: vertical guidance, UHF 329–335 MHz, usually 3°|Markers or DME for range|Categories (CAT I, II, III) and their minima

interview.question: What is the effect of high temperature and high elevation on take-off performance?
interview.covers: Lower air density → less lift and less engine thrust|Longer take-off run and poorer climb|Density altitude concept|Hot-and-high airports, possible weight limits

interview.question: What is a jet stream and why does it matter to us?
interview.covers: Narrow band of very strong wind near the tropopause|Saves time and fuel with a tailwind, costs with a headwind|Clear air turbulence near its edges|Subtropical jet over north India in winter

interview.question: Tell us about the hazards of a thunderstorm.
interview.covers: Turbulence, icing, hail, lightning, microbursts and wind shear|Stay at least 20 NM away from severe storms|Never fly underneath a CB on approach|Use weather radar and ATC deviations

interview.question: What is wind shear and how would you recover from it on approach?
interview.covers: Sudden change in wind speed or direction|Microbursts below CBs are the most dangerous|Recovery: TOGA power, pitch to the guidance (or about 15°), don't change configuration, follow through till clear|Report it to ATC

interview.question: What is the difference between an aerodrome's TORA, TODA and ASDA?
interview.covers: TORA: runway length available for the ground run|TODA: TORA plus clearway|ASDA: TORA plus stopway|Used to check take-off and accelerate-stop distances

interview.question: What is RVSM and what equipment does an aircraft need for it?
interview.covers: Reduced Vertical Separation Minimum: 1,000 ft between FL290 and FL410|Two independent altimeters, autopilot with altitude hold, altitude alerter, Mode C/S transponder|Needs approval for the aircraft and the operator

interview.question: Tell us about yourself.
interview.covers: About 90 seconds: who you are, your training, a highlight, why this job|Keep it professional and positive|End with why you're ready for this airline

interview.question: Why do you want to fly for us?
interview.covers: Name real things about the airline: fleet, network, safety record, culture|Link them to your own goals|Avoid 'because you're hiring' or salary

interview.question: Where do you see yourself in five years?
interview.covers: Building experience as a first officer and becoming a strong team member|Command upgrade as a longer goal|Shows loyalty and realistic ambition

interview.question: What are your strengths and weaknesses?
interview.covers: One real strength with a quick example|One real weakness and what you're doing about it|Avoid fake weaknesses like 'I work too hard'

interview.question: How do you handle criticism from a senior pilot?
interview.covers: Listen, don't argue in the moment|Take what's useful, ask questions to understand|Debrief calmly if you disagree|Example from training

interview.question: What do you know about our fleet and where we fly?
interview.covers: Main aircraft type(s) and roughly how many|Main bases and a few key routes, domestic and international|Recent news (new aircraft, new routes)|Shows you prepared

interview.question: Why should we choose you over the other candidates?
interview.covers: Two or three specific qualities with evidence|Safety mindset, teamwork, adaptability|Don't put others down

interview.question: How do you balance this job with the irregular hours?
interview.covers: Understand rosters, nights and time away|Good rest habits, fitness and a support system|Shows you've thought it through

interview.question: What does 'safety culture' mean to you?
interview.covers: Everyone reports mistakes and hazards without fear (just culture)|Following SOPs even when no one is watching|Learning from incidents|An example of you reporting or speaking up

interview.question: Tell us about a time you worked in a team that wasn't getting along.
interview.covers: STAR format|What you did to help: listening, clarifying roles, staying calm|Result and what you learned

interview.question: How do you keep your knowledge current while waiting for a job?
interview.covers: Revising technical subjects and SOPs|Simulator sessions or type-rating prep|Reading safety reports and aviation news|Keeping licence and medical valid

interview.question: Do you have any questions for us?
interview.covers: Always have one or two ready|Ask about training, the first year on the line, or culture|Avoid asking about pay in the first interview
